sentences: She found the local shopping centre the most efficient place to complete all errands in one trip.
He found the large regional shopping centres reshaping suburban retail across Australia.
A shopping centre is a large building housing multiple retail stores, food outlets, and services.
She found shopping centres in Australia operating from nine in the morning to five-thirty on most days — with extended trading Thursday evenings.
He found the major shopping centre groups — Westfield, Chadstone, Pacific Fair — the most significant retail destinations.
Shopping centres in Australia often anchor larger developments including car parks and apartments.
She found the shopping centre food court the most culturally diverse eating environment in her suburb.
He found supermarkets as the anchor tenants driving foot traffic to surrounding specialty stores.
Shopping centres serve as community hubs — particularly in suburban areas with limited public space.
She describes the shopping centre as the place she went to for everything practical and left from with more than intended.
She found Australian consumer rights among the strongest in the world — the ACL was comprehensive.
He found consumer rights applying to goods and services purchased from businesses.
Consumer rights are the legal protections afforded to people who buy goods and services.
She found the Australian Consumer Law — ACL — the primary national consumer protection framework.
He found consumer rights including guarantees for quality, fitness for purpose, and acceptable appearance.
Consumer rights in Australia cannot be signed away by fine print — they are non-negotiable.
She found consumer rights applying to online purchases as well as in-store transactions.
He found the ACCC and state fair trading offices enforcing consumer rights.
Consumer rights include the right to a remedy — repair, replacement, or refund depending on the fault.
She describes understanding consumer rights as the knowledge that most changed how confidently she made purchases.
She requested a refund after the appliance stopped working within the warranty period.
He found his right to a refund under the Australian Consumer Law clear — the item had a major fault.
A refund is the return of money paid for a product or service when the consumer is entitled to one.
She found refunds required when goods had a major failure — not just an inconvenience.
He found retailers required to provide a remedy — repair, replacement, or refund — for faulty goods.
Refunds in Australia are a legal entitlement — not a policy decision that stores can override.
She found stores incorrectly claiming no refund on sale items — an illegal practice.
He found the ACCC website clarifying his refund rights before approaching the retailer.
Refunds on change of mind are at the retailer's discretion — but faulty goods are a legal right.
She describes claiming a refund on a major fault as a calm, factual exercise once she knew her rights.
She lodged a complaint with the ACCC after the business refused to honour her consumer guarantee.
He found the ACCC the national regulator for consumer protection, competition, and fair trading.
The ACCC — Australian Competition and Consumer Commission — enforces the Australian Consumer Law.
She found the ACCC website the best source of plain-language consumer rights information.
He found the ACCC taking action against businesses making misleading claims — the penalties were significant.
The ACCC investigates anti-competitive behaviour, cartels, and misleading advertising.
She found the ACCC Scamwatch database invaluable for identifying and reporting consumer scams.
He found the ACCC's product recall database listing unsafe products — he checked before buying used goods.
The ACCC works alongside state and territory fair trading offices on consumer matters.
She describes the ACCC as the institution that most made her feel Australian commerce operated within fair rules.
She checked the product recall database before continuing to use the baby carrier she had bought second-hand.
He found the ACCC's product recall portal listing thousands of recalled consumer products.
A product recall is when a business or regulator withdraws a product due to safety concerns.
She found recalls covering children's toys, electrical goods, food, and vehicles.
He found businesses legally required to notify the ACCC when recalling a consumer product.
Product recall notices appear on the ACCC website and are issued directly to known purchasers.
She found registering products after purchase ensuring she received recall notices directly.
He found product recalls in Australia covering voluntary recalls by businesses and mandatory recalls by regulators.
Product recalls protect consumers from injury — she took them seriously after finding a recalled blender in her kitchen.
She describes checking the recall database as the five-minute habit that gave her the most peace of mind.
She found the Australian Consumer Law applying uniformly across all states — no patchwork of different rules.
He found the Australian Consumer Law the single most important document for understanding shopping rights.
The Australian Consumer Law — ACL — is the national framework providing consumer guarantees and protections.
She found the ACL applying to most goods and services purchased in Australia.
He found the ACL prohibiting misleading conduct, unconscionable behaviour, and unfair contract terms.
The Australian Consumer Law is set out in Schedule 2 of the Competition and Consumer Act 2010.
She found the ACL guarantees applying regardless of what the retailer's own policy stated.
He found the ACL distinguishing between minor and major failures — each attracting different remedies.
The Australian Consumer Law was introduced in 2011 to replace a patchwork of state and territory laws.
She describes the Australian Consumer Law as the legislation she most wished had been explained to her when she first arrived.
She put the pram on layby — she paid it off over three months before taking it home.
He found layby the most sensible way to plan a significant purchase without using credit.
A layby is an arrangement where a consumer pays for an item in instalments and collects it when fully paid.
She found layby not involving credit — she never paid interest.
He found layby particularly useful for Christmas gifts — spreading the cost across October and November.
Layby agreements in Australia are covered by the Australian Consumer Law — cancellation rights apply.
She found layby still offered by Kmart, Target, and some independent retailers.
He found layby providing the discipline of saving without the temptation of buy now pay later debt.
Layby cancellation fees are limited by the ACL — retailers cannot charge more than their reasonable costs.
She describes layby as the shopping arrangement that most aligned with her financial values.
She uses Afterpay occasionally — she found it useful when cash flow was tight between pay cycles.
He found Afterpay the most widely adopted buy now pay later service in Australia.
Afterpay is a financial service allowing purchases to be split into four fortnightly payments.
She found Afterpay not charging interest — but late fees applied if payments were missed.
He found Afterpay used across fashion, electronics, and health retailers in Australia.
Afterpay was founded in Australia in 2015 — it became a global platform before being acquired by Square.
She found consumer advocates warning that Afterpay could normalise spending beyond means.
He found Afterpay spending now subject to credit reporting changes — missed payments tracked.
Afterpay is available both in-store and online — she used it predominantly for online purchases.
She describes Afterpay as the service that made spending feel less immediate — a feature and a warning.
She consolidated her spending onto one loyalty program — Flybuys — to accumulate points faster.
He found Australian loyalty programs Flybuys and Everyday Rewards the most widely held.
A loyalty program rewards customers for repeat purchases with points, discounts, or benefits.
She found the loyalty program data collection more significant than the rewards it offered.
He found loyalty program points redeemable for flights, gift cards, and grocery discounts.
Loyalty programs in Australia are operated by supermarkets, airlines, banks, and retailers.
She found Frequent Flyer and Velocity programs the most valuable for regular domestic travellers.
He found the loyalty program terms changing regularly — she read the updates carefully.
Loyalty programs represent a data exchange — the consumer trades personal information for rewards.
She describes the loyalty program as the deal that seemed better before she understood what she was trading.
She asked for a price match at the electronics store — the competitor's price was twenty dollars less.
He found price matching commonly offered by JB Hi-Fi, Harvey Norman, and major appliance retailers.
Price matching is the practice of a retailer agreeing to sell at a competitor's lower advertised price.
She found price matching only applicable to identical items — same model, same specifications.
He found the price match request most effective when the competitor's ad was shown in person.
Price matching in Australia is a voluntary policy — not a legal requirement.
She found the price match saving her forty dollars on a camera lens — worth the thirty-second conversation.
He found online prices sometimes excluded from price match policies — he read the terms.
Price matching reduces the need to shop around if a retailer is committed to the policy.
She describes price matching as the negotiation she most appreciated having the confidence to attempt.
She found end-of-financial-year clearance sales the best time to buy furniture and appliances.
He found clearance sales in January — post-Christmas — and June — end of financial year — the most significant.
A clearance sale is a retail event where stock is sold at reduced prices to clear inventory.
She found clearance prices sometimes as low as eighty percent off the original retail price.
He found clearance items often non-returnable — he inspected carefully before purchasing.
Clearance sales in Australian retail are most significant around Christmas, Easter, and EOFY.
She found department stores managing clearance through a dedicated section rather than a timed event.
He found clearance sales online easier to navigate than in-store — filtering by discount percentage.
Clearance stock may be discontinued, cosmetically imperfect, or last season — worth understanding which.
She describes the clearance sale as the retail moment that most required patience — and knowledge of the original price.
She bought her laptop during the EOFY sale — it was fifty percent off and she needed it for work.
He found EOFY sales in June the most practical time to buy equipment eligible for tax deduction.
An EOFY sale — End of Financial Year sale — occurs in late June, timed to the Australian financial year-end.
She found EOFY sales most significant in electronics, cars, and office equipment.
He found purchasing before 30 June ensuring tax deductions applied in the current financial year.
EOFY sales are also driven by retailers needing to clear stock before the new financial year.
She found EOFY sale prices comparable to or better than Boxing Day sales for technology.
He found businesses making purchases in the EOFY window claiming immediate tax deductions on eligible items.
EOFY sales are advertised heavily from mid-May — she planned her list in advance.
She describes the EOFY sale as the annual event that most rewarded having a shopping list prepared.
She read the returns policy before buying the dress online — change of mind returns were free.
He found generous returns policies among the most important factors in choosing an online retailer.
A returns policy is the set of rules a retailer uses to manage product returns and refunds.
She found returns policies varying widely — some offering thirty days, others ninety.
He found returns policies for change of mind purchases discretionary — for faulty goods, the ACL applied.
Returns policies in Australia cannot override legal consumer guarantees — the law supersedes policy.
She found the returns policy for large purchases particularly important — appliances and furniture.
He found keeping receipts essential for returns — she photographed every receipt on her phone.
Returns policies for online purchases include the right to refuse accepting certain goods back.
She describes the returns policy as the fine print that most determined whether she trusted the retailer.
She sold the furniture on Facebook Marketplace before the move — faster and easier than expected.
He found online marketplaces the most efficient channel for buying and selling second-hand goods.
A marketplace is a platform where multiple buyers and sellers transact — physical or digital.
She found Amazon, eBay, and Facebook Marketplace the dominant online marketplaces in Australia.
He found Australian-operated marketplaces including Gumtree and Trading Post.
Marketplaces operate differently from direct retailers — the platform connects parties but may not be the seller.
She found marketplace consumer protections applying differently — the ACCC clarified the rules.
He found marketplace buying requiring more due diligence than retail — especially for high-value items.
Marketplaces generate income through commissions, listing fees, or advertising.
She describes the marketplace as the trading environment that most changed how she thought about ownership and consumption.
She gave a gift card to avoid guessing the wrong size — practical and appreciated.
He found Australian law requiring gift cards to be valid for at least three years.
A gift card is a prepaid card loaded with a set value — redeemable at specific retailers.
She found the three-year minimum expiry rule a significant consumer protection — gift cards used to expire in months.
He found gift card purchases during sales — such as discount gift card promotions — a savvy way to save.
Gift cards in Australia cannot charge post-purchase fees — the law prohibits them.
She found the law requiring remaining balances visible at all times on digital gift cards.
He found gift cards the most common Australian birthday gift when the recipient was difficult to buy for.
Gift card refunds are not required by law — the card is treated as a cash equivalent.
She describes gift card reform as the consumer protection she most appreciated — ending the era of expiring generosity.
She does most of her shopping online — it fits her schedule and she finds better prices.
He found online shopping in Australia transformed by the COVID period — adoption accelerated significantly.
Online shopping is the purchase of goods and services over the internet for delivery or collection.
She found Australian online shopping growing significantly — particularly post-2020.
He found international online retailers — Amazon, ASOS, and others — shipping to Australia efficiently.
Online shopping in Australia is protected by the ACL — consumer guarantees apply regardless of channel.
She found click and collect the most convenient option — purchased online, collected within hours.
He found GST applied to international online purchases above a thousand dollars.
Online shopping creates challenges — sizing, colour accuracy, and return logistics.
She describes online shopping as the retail format that most required her to develop judgment about what she could trust.
She found next-day delivery available in major Australian cities — regional areas took longer.
He found delivery fees a significant addition to Australian online shopping costs.
Delivery is the transportation of purchased goods to the buyer's nominated address.
She found Australia Post, Startrack, and Aramex the dominant domestic delivery services.
He found delivery tracking the feature that most reduced his anxiety about online purchases.
Delivery in regional and remote Australia is more expensive and slower — a geographic disadvantage.
She found free delivery thresholds — spend over fifty dollars and delivery is included.
He found safe drop becoming the default — parcels left at the door when no one was home.
Delivery timeframes in Australia vary significantly — express delivery is a premium option.
She describes the delivery notification as the text message that most reliably improved her afternoon.
She received a scam text message claiming her parcel was held — she did not click the link.
He found scam losses in Australia totalling over three billion dollars annually.
A scam is a fraudulent scheme designed to trick people into giving money or personal information.
She found Scamwatch — run by the ACCC — the best place to report and research scams.
He found the most common Australian scams involving fake parcel delivery, investment fraud, and romance scams.
Scams in Australia exploit urgency, fear, and the desire for a deal.
She found scam text messages accurately spoofing legitimate bank and government numbers.
He found scam losses disproportionately affecting older Australians and recent migrants.
Scams are reported to Scamwatch, the ACCC, and relevant platforms — and should always be reported.
She describes the scam she almost fell for as the experience that most changed her approach to unsolicited digital contact.
She found consumer guarantees applying automatically under Australian law — no registration required.
He found consumer guarantees more powerful than manufacturer warranties in most cases.
A consumer guarantee is a legally enforceable standard that goods and services must meet.
She found consumer guarantees covering acceptable quality, fit for purpose, and matching description.
He found consumer guarantees applying for a reasonable time — not just the manufacturer's stated period.
Consumer guarantees in Australia cannot be excluded by contract — they are mandatory.
She found consumer guarantees applying when a good did not last as long as one would reasonably expect.
He found the distinction between minor and major failures critical — major failures meant she could refuse a repair and demand a refund.
Consumer guarantees apply to both goods and services — a poorly delivered service is also covered.
She describes consumer guarantees as the legal floor that most gave her confidence to buy without fear.
She contacted NSW Fair Trading after the builder refused to rectify the defective work.
He found state fair trading offices the most accessible consumer complaint pathway for local disputes.
Fair trading refers to commerce conducted within legal and ethical standards protecting consumers.
She found Fair Trading offices in each state and territory — the state-level equivalent of the ACCC.
He found NSW Fair Trading, Consumer Affairs Victoria, and Queensland's Office of Fair Trading the main state bodies.
Fair trading offices handle complaints about local businesses, traders, and service providers.
She found fair trading mediation the most practical resolution for a building dispute.
He found fair trading laws prohibiting unconscionable conduct — exploiting someone's vulnerability.
Fair trading offices also provide tenancy dispute resolution in most Australian states.
She describes contacting Fair Trading as the step that most quickly shifted the dynamic in her dispute.
She orders click and collect at the hardware store — ready within two hours.
He found click and collect eliminating delivery fees and wait times simultaneously.
Click and collect is a retail service where goods are ordered online and collected in-store.
She found click and collect most useful for bulky items that were impractical to ship.
He found click and collect the format most adopted by Australian supermarkets during peak demand.
Click and collect typically costs less than home delivery — often free.
She found the turnaround time for click and collect improving — some retailers offering one-hour readiness.
He found click and collect solving the problem of being home to receive a delivery.
Click and collect allowed her to check the item before leaving the store — she could raise issues immediately.
She describes click and collect as the shopping format that most elegantly combined online convenience with in-person certainty.
She found price gouging complaints surge during natural disasters when essential goods were scarce.
He found the ACCC monitoring price gouging in fuel, groceries, and essential services.
Price gouging is the practice of raising prices to unfair levels during periods of high demand or crisis.
She found Australian consumer law not providing a universal price cap — but unconscionable conduct provisions applied.
He found supermarket price gouging a major concern raised by the ACCC's 2024 inquiry.
Price gouging on hand sanitiser and face masks during COVID prompted government and public backlash.
She found price gouging at petrol stations before public holidays subject to ACCC scrutiny.
He found price gouging most harmful to lower-income households — they could not substitute or delay.
Price gouging in essential services — water, energy, groceries — is the form most concerning to Australian regulators.
She describes learning about price gouging as the consumer education that most explained why she felt frustrated at the checkout.
She found the supermarket duopoly — Woolworths and Coles — dominating Australian grocery retail.
He found the supermarket duopoly controlling approximately sixty-five percent of Australian grocery spending.
A supermarket duopoly is a market dominated by two large retailers with limited competition.
She found the ACCC's 2024 supermarket inquiry examining pricing practices, buyer power, and supplier treatment.
He found the duopoly's private label products undercutting branded goods — supplier margins squeezed.
The supermarket duopoly in Australia has faced persistent criticism for profit margins and treatment of suppliers.
She found the Senate inquiry into supermarkets the most politically charged consumer policy debate of the year.
He found Aldi and IGA providing some competitive discipline — but the duopoly's market share remained dominant.
The supermarket duopoly's buyer power affects the prices farmers received for produce.
She describes the supermarket duopoly as the market structure that most directly affected what she paid for her weekly groceries.
She found GST included in displayed prices in most Australian retail — ten percent on most goods.
He found the GST exempting fresh food, medical products, and education in most forms.
GST — Goods and Services Tax — is a ten percent tax applied to most goods and services in Australia.
She found GST included in the shelf price — not added at checkout as in some other countries.
He found businesses with annual turnover above seventy-five thousand dollars required to register for GST.
GST was introduced in Australia on 1 July 2000 — replacing a complex system of wholesale taxes.
She found tax invoices displaying the GST component separately — important for business expense claims.
He found GST not applying to exports — businesses could claim GST back on exported goods.
GST revenue is distributed to states and territories under the federation funding arrangement.
She describes understanding GST as the tax knowledge that most helped her understand Australian business pricing.
She uses a cashback credit card — one percent returned on all spending adds up.
He found cashback websites and apps offering returns on online purchases.
Cashback is a financial incentive where a portion of a purchase price is returned to the consumer.
She found cashback credit cards offering between one and two percent on general spending.
He found cashback offers on major purchases — insurance, utilities, and electronics — through comparison websites.
Cashback through credit cards only provides value if the balance is paid in full — interest erases the benefit.
She found cashback portal ShopBack popular in Australia for online retail purchases.
He found cashback on energy switching the most underused saving available to Australian households.
Cashback is a marketing tool — the cost is factored into pricing by the retailer.
She describes the cashback program she joined as the financial habit that most rewarded the spending she was already doing.
She checks the expiry date on the product before buying — particularly for supplements and skincare.
He found expiry dates on food, medicine, and cosmetics carrying different legal implications.
An expiry date is the date after which a product is no longer considered safe or effective.
She found expired medicines returned to the chemist through the Return Unwanted Medicines program.
He found the distinction between expiry date and best before date important for food safety.
Expiry dates on medicines and certain foods carry strict safety implications — not merely quality.
She found food past its expiry date legally unable to be sold in Australia.
He found sunscreen and certain over-the-counter medicines losing efficacy after expiry — not merely a guideline.
Expiry dates on gift cards were prohibited in Australia — a consumer protection reform.
She describes checking expiry dates as the shopping habit that most saved her from both food waste and safety risk.
She compares products using unit pricing — the per-hundred-gram cost makes the decision simple.
He found unit pricing on supermarket shelves the most useful information for comparing value.
Unit pricing is the display of the price per standard unit — per hundred grams, per litre — alongside the retail price.
She found unit pricing required by law in large supermarkets in Australia.
He found unit pricing revealing that the larger size was not always better value.
Unit pricing in Australia must be displayed prominently — the law specifies the font size and format.
She found unit pricing the single most practical tool for grocery comparison shopping.
He found unit pricing applied to loose produce, packaged goods, and bulk items.
Unit pricing comparisons are only valid within the same product category and measurement unit.
She describes unit pricing as the shelf label she most trained herself to read before the retail price.
She got a trade-in value on her old phone — two hundred dollars off the new one.
He found trade-in programs at Apple, Samsung, and Telstra offering the best values.
A trade-in is an arrangement where an old item is given to a retailer in exchange for a discount on a new purchase.
She found trade-in values varying significantly — she compared three retailers before deciding.
He found car trade-ins the largest category — the old vehicle offset against the new car purchase price.
Trade-in programs reduce the environmental impact of disposal — older devices refurbished or recycled.
She found trade-in values contingent on condition — cracked screens reduced the offer significantly.
He found the trade-in offer best accepted at the time of a new purchase — not later.
Trade-ins create a resale market — some trade-in items are cleaned and sold as certified refurbished.
She describes accepting a trade-in offer as the transaction that most made her feel practical rather than sentimental about her old phone.
She found the manufacturer's warranty extending the period in which faults could be repaired for free.
He found the warranty period varying — one year for electronics, five for appliances, ten for some tools.
A warranty is a manufacturer's promise to repair or replace a product within a specified period.
She found manufacturer warranties supplemented by — but not replacing — consumer guarantees under the ACL.
He found extended warranties offered at point of sale — often overpriced relative to failure rates.
Warranties in Australia must be honoured — failing to do so is a breach of the ACL.
She found the warranty terms important: whether it covered parts only, or parts and labour.
He found the warranty registration process quick — and worth completing to ensure coverage.
Warranties and consumer guarantees coexist — consumer guarantees may last longer than the stated warranty.
She describes understanding the difference between a warranty and a consumer guarantee as the knowledge that most changed how she handled product failures.
She requested a bill of sale when buying the second-hand car from the private seller.
He found a bill of sale essential for high-value private transactions — motorbikes, trailers, and boats.
A bill of sale is a written document confirming the transfer of ownership of goods from seller to buyer.
She found a bill of sale important for demonstrating legitimate acquisition if questions arose later.
He found the bill of sale including the parties' names, date, description, and agreed price.
Bills of sale are particularly important for unregistered vehicles and private party transactions.
She found template bills of sale available through state consumer affairs offices.
He found signing a bill of sale providing both parties with legal clarity about the transaction.
A bill of sale is not required for most retail purchases — receipts serve the same purpose.
She describes the bill of sale as the document she most valued when the car she bought turned out to have a history.
She found the department store the most convenient single stop for clothing, homewares, and cosmetics.
He found Australian department stores — Myer and David Jones — under ongoing commercial pressure.
A department store is a large retail outlet selling a wide variety of goods in distinct sections.
She found Myer and David Jones the two surviving national Australian department store chains.
He found department stores most compelling during sales events — significant discounts on quality brands.
Department stores in Australia have contracted — many stores closed as online competition grew.
She found the cosmetics floor of the department store the most theatrical retail environment she visited.
He found department store credit cards offering exclusive loyalty benefits — she evaluated carefully.
Department stores provide a curated shopping experience — brands available in one location.
She describes the department store as the retail format she visited most nostalgically — and least frequently.
She found the outlet store selling last season's designer items at forty percent discount.
He found Birkenhead Point and DFO the most well-known outlet shopping centres in Australia.
An outlet store sells discontinued, overstocked, or previous season goods at reduced prices.
She found outlet stores offering genuine brands at significant savings — she verified authenticity.
He found DFO — Direct Factory Outlet — centres in Brisbane, Melbourne, Sydney, and Perth.
Outlet stores carry irregular or last-season stock — she found the range limited but the savings significant.
She found outlet shopping worth the travel to a regional or airport location.
He found some outlet stores carrying items made specifically for the outlet channel — not genuine surplus.
Outlet stores combine the brand experience with clearance pricing — a model that attracted significant foot traffic.
She describes outlet shopping as the retail format that most rewarded the patience to sift rather than the habit of buying on impulse.
She photographs every receipt on her phone — it replaced a shoebox of paper slips.
He found keeping receipts the single most important consumer habit for managing returns and claims.
A receipt is a document confirming a purchase transaction — the record of what was paid.
She found digital receipts emailed automatically from many Australian retailers.
He found receipts essential for warranty claims, tax deductions, and returns.
Receipts in Australia must be provided for transactions over seventy-five dollars — mandatory.
She found e-receipts reducing paper waste — she opted in wherever the option was offered.
He found the ATO accepting photographed receipts as valid records for tax purposes.
Receipts also serve as proof of purchase in the event of a consumer guarantee dispute.
She describes the receipt as the document she most consistently undervalued — until she needed one.
She found the stocktake sale at the furniture store clearing last year's models at half price.
He found stocktake sales most common in January and June in Australian retail.
A stocktake sale is a retail event where goods are discounted to reduce inventory before a count.
She found stocktake sales at independent retailers offering more genuine discounts than chain promotions.
He found stocktake sales on flooring, furniture, and electrical goods the most significant.
Stocktake sales help retailers understand and reduce their inventory before the next season.
She found the stocktake sale signs reliable indicators of genuine discounting — not manufactured urgency.
He found stocktake sale items sometimes the last of their kind — no restock expected.
Stocktake sales benefit both retailer — reduced carrying cost — and consumer — lower prices.
She describes the stocktake sale as the retail event she most planned around — noting dates in advance.
She reported misleading advertising after the product did not match its television commercial.
He found misleading advertising prohibited by the Australian Consumer Law and enforced by the ACCC.
Misleading advertising is promotional material that creates a false impression in consumers' minds.
She found greenwashing — false environmental claims — the most common form of misleading advertising she encountered.
He found the ACCC successfully prosecuting businesses for misleading fuel economy and ingredient claims.
Misleading advertising includes false price comparisons — the was/now format misused to suggest savings that weren't real.
She found the advertised claims for superfoods among the most misleadingly phrased she had evaluated.
He found the ACCC's education campaign on misleading advertising improving consumer awareness.
Misleading advertising undermines market trust — it distorts decision-making and rewards dishonest competitors.
She describes identifying misleading advertising as the critical thinking exercise that most sharpened her as a consumer.
